zh_title: 让美军留在北约驻科部队

content:
随着五角大楼最终完成对美国在欧洲的军事态势的审查，一项相对较小的承诺值得避免预算削减：即在北约科索沃部队服役的约 600 名美国士兵。他们几乎没有参与关于旅和数十亿美元项目的辩论，但他们在巴尔干地区保持了来之不易的和平，将他们撤出几乎什么也挽救不了，同时让莫斯科获得了廉价的战略胜利。驻科部队于 1999 年 6 月在北约指挥下部署，此前北约轰炸了南斯拉夫，以制止斯洛博丹·米洛舍维奇领导的塞尔维亚军队对阿尔巴尼亚人的暴力行为。科索沃于2008年宣布独立，但塞尔维亚在俄罗斯和中国的支持下仍然拒绝承认。欧洲态势评估是一项合法的活动。在多年来敦促欧洲盟国承担更多常规防御之后，特朗普政府正确地提出了一些尖锐的问题，即美国军队在哪些方面可以增加独特的价值，以及在适当的时间发展其能力和能力的情况下欧洲可以在哪些方面加强。但驻科部队是一项美国角色不易被取代的任务，因为它既是政治性的，也是军事性的，而且错误的决定可能会导致欧洲东南侧的不稳定。从威胁开始。即使在乌克兰遭受重大损失的同时，弗拉基米尔·普京也没有放弃破坏欧洲稳定的努力。巴尔干地区是欧洲的软肋，是一个备受青睐的舞台：煽动成本低廉，是一个分散西方对乌克兰注意力的地方。
莫斯科长期以来一直利用塞尔维亚作为破坏科索沃稳定的杠杆。2017年，一列俄罗斯制造的火车开往科索沃北部，这是一次带有“科索沃是塞尔维亚”口号的滚动挑衅。俄罗斯在科索沃附近运营着一个所谓的人道主义中心，该中心被怀疑充当俄罗斯情报站。塞尔维亚与俄罗斯密切的情报联系使莫斯科能够接触到准备挑衅的当地民族主义力量。 2023年，科索沃北部警察遭到武装袭击，普里什蒂纳将此归咎于塞尔维亚支持的武装分子，这加剧了人们对与俄罗斯结盟的行为体利用紧张局势的担忧；今年早些时候，俄罗斯外交部长警告称，“欧洲中心正在酝酿一场重大爆炸性局势”。紧张局势一再爆发。 2023年5月，塞尔维亚抗议者与科索沃警察发生冲突，造成90多名北约维和人员受伤，促使塞尔维亚提高军事戒备级别。那年 9 月，在巴尼斯卡发生的一次袭击中，全副武装的塞族枪手杀死了一名科索沃警察，并将自己关在一座修道院里，这表明当地的冲突可以多么迅速地演变为地区危机。危险还没有过去。塞尔维亚强人亚历山大·武契奇承认在10月25日的塞尔维亚议会选举中落败，但贝尔格莱德的外交政策方向尚不确定，人们担心其对科索沃的看法不会改变。
十月，俄罗斯驻联合国大使警告说，科索沃局势“仍然持续紧张，甚至濒临崩溃”。尽管如此，科索沃和塞尔维亚自 1999 年以来一直保持和平，这在很大程度上要归功于驻科部队。用美国两党议员团体的话说，这支部队的作用是“对那些试图煽动种族暴力的人起到政治威慑作用”。美国从驻科部队撤军可能会助长科索沃和塞尔维亚的民族主义议程，以及波斯尼亚附近塞族统治地区塞族共和国的分裂主义野心。美国在驻科部队中的存在之所以受到重视，正是因为

【原文 English Original】
As the Pentagon finalizes its review of U.S. force posture in Europe, one relatively small commitment deserves protection from the budget axe: the roughly 600 American troops serving in NATO’s Kosovo Force. They barely register in a debate about brigades and billion-dollar line items, but they keep a hard-won peace in the Balkans, and pulling them out would save almost nothing while handing Moscow a cheap strategic win. KFOR was deployed in June 1999 under NATO command, after the alliance bombed Yugoslavia to stop the violence perpetrated by Slobodan Milosevic’s Serbian forces against ethnic Albanians. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, but Serbia, backed by Russia and China, still refuses to recognize it. The Europe posture review is a legitimate exercise. After years of urging European allies to shoulder more of their own conventional defense, the Trump administration is right to ask hard questions about where American forces add unique value and where Europe can step up given suitable time to develop their capabilities and capacities. But KFOR is a mission in which the American role is not easily replaced, because it is as much political as military, and where a wrong call risks instability on Europe’s southeastern flank. Start with the threat. Even while absorbing heavy losses in Ukraine, Vladimir Putin has not given up on destabilizing Europe. The Balkans, Europe’s soft underbelly, are a favored arena: cheap to stir, a place to distract Western attention from Ukraine. Moscow has long used Serbia as a lever against Kosovo’s stability. In 2017, a Russian-made train was sent toward northern Kosovo, a rolling provocation that bore the slogan “Kosovo is Serbia.” Russia runs a so-called humanitarian center near Kosovo that is suspected of serving as a Russian intelligence station. Close Serbian-Russian intelligence ties give Moscow access to local nationalist forces prepared for provocations. In 2023, an armed attack on Kosovo police in the north, which Pristina blamed on Serbian-backed militants, heightened fears that Russian-aligned actors were exploiting the tension; earlier that year, Russia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs warned that “a major explosive situation is brewing in the heart of Europe.” Tensions have repeatedly flared. In May 2023, clashes between Serb protesters and Kosovo police injured more than 90 NATO peacekeepers and prompted Serbia to raise its military alert level. That September, an attack in Banjska, where heavily armed Serb gunmen killed a Kosovo police officer and barricaded themselves in a monastery, showed how quickly a local flare-up can become a regional crisis. The danger has not passed. Serbian strongman Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Serbia’s Oct. 25 parliamentary election, but Belgrade’s foreign-policy direction is uncertain and there are concerns that its views on Kosovo will not change. In October, Russia’s ambassador to the UN warned that the situation in Kosovo “remains persistently tense and is literally teetering on the brink.” Still, Kosovo and Serbia have remained at peace since 1999, in large part because of KFOR. In the words of a bipartisan group of U.S lawmakers, the force functions as “a political deterrent to those seeking to stoke ethnic violence.” An American drawdown from KFOR may embolden nationalist agendas in Kosovo and Serbia as well as separatist ambitions in Republika Srpska, the Serb-dominated region in nearby Bosnia. The American presence in KFOR is valued precisely because it is American. U.S. troops have anchored KFOR since its creation, and Washington currently leads Regional Command East, a position of real operational weight, not symbolism. The U.S. has traditionally provided the 600 or so American troops—often Army National Guardsmen—an economy-of-force mission with minimal cost or effect on the U.S. Army’s ability to execute missions elsewhere around the globe. The mission accounts for less than 1 percent of the total U.S. troops in Europe. KFOR’s value becomes plain when contrasted with Operation Althea in neighboring Bosnia. EUFOR, an EU-led force with roughly 1,500 troops, has struggled to respond decisively to repeated provocations by Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik, who’s backed by Moscow and Belgrade. EU ambassadors rejected Bosnian appeals to help enforce an arrest warrant against him in 2025, citing political risk. Dodik has openly mocked EUFOR’s patrols. Lacking an American anchor and a unified chain of command willing to act, EUFOR has too often had to manage crises rather than deterring them. KFOR, by contrast, has demonstrated it can surge forces when tested, providing genuine deterrence. After the 2023 Banjska incident, NATO increased its peacekeeping presence in Kosovo. Serbia drew down its border deployment, ending the crisis. The Pentagon is right to ask what the value of an American military presence is worth. For KFOR, the answer is plain: a few hundred U.S. troops are successfully maintaining a quarter-century-long peace that Russia would love to see unravel. Lawmakers from both parties already understand that. The Pentagon should, too, and keep KFOR intact. Mark Montgomery, a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral, serves as a senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ (FDD), where Ivana Stradner is a research fellow. ]]>

title: Destroyer returns from 11-month-deployment
zh_title: 驱逐舰结束 11 个月的部署返回
summary: 夏威夷珍珠港——导弹驱逐舰迈克尔·墨菲号在经过 346 天的部署（其中包括在南中国海的行动、12 次有争议地穿越霍尔木兹海峡、43 次海上补给以及 10 个月后撤换其指挥官）之后于周四返航，受到了草裙舞者和海峡上空延伸的彩虹的欢迎。尽管这艘航空母舰于 10 月 8 日返回圣地亚哥基地，但其大部分部署时间都隶属于亚伯拉罕·林肯号航母打击群。但它可能打破的任何部署长度记录都是短暂的。斯普鲁亚
content:
夏威夷珍珠港——导弹驱逐舰迈克尔·墨菲号在经过 346 天的部署（其中包括在南中国海的行动、12 次有争议地穿越霍尔木兹海峡、43 次海上补给以及 10 个月后撤换其指挥官）之后于周四返航，受到了草裙舞者和海峡上空延伸的彩虹的欢迎。尽管这艘航空母舰于 10 月 8 日返回圣地亚哥基地，但其大部分部署时间都隶属于亚伯拉罕·林肯号航母打击群。但它可能打破的任何部署长度记录都是短暂的。另一艘阿利伯克级驱逐舰斯普鲁恩斯号在经过 12 个月的部署后于今天返回家园，驻日本的约翰·芬恩号船员被告知预计将进行 13 至 14 个月的部署。正如《防务一号》10 月 22 日报道的那样，海军官员告诉家属，在可预见的未来，部署时间预计为 10 到 10 个月，这与近几十年来典型的 7 个月部署形成鲜明对比。海军最高军士长、海军军士长约翰·佩里曼 (John Perryman) 一周后证实了这一点，并表示至少在未来几年内，10 至 11 个月将成为常态。迈克尔·墨菲号中校表示，“迈克尔·墨菲”号于 2025 年 12 月 1 日离开夏威夷，穿过南中国海和马六甲海峡，然后到达北阿拉伯海，并在那里度过了大部分部署时间。大卫·尼古拉斯一个月前接任这艘驱逐舰的指挥。
尼古拉斯说，“迈克尔·墨菲”号在“史诗狂怒”行动期间发动了“战斧”导弹袭击，并参与了霍尔木兹海峡的封锁。“我非常自豪能够成为这个团队的一员，”他说。 “这是我有幸共事过的最有韧性的团队。”尼古拉斯此前指挥过另一艘导弹驱逐舰奥斯卡·奥斯汀号。据海军新闻稿称，当他于 9 月 10 日将掌权交给继任者时，他将成为罗德岛州水面作战学校的教官。但一名海军官员向《防务一号》证实，当“迈克尔·墨菲”号的前任上司中校改变了他的计划。凯特琳·坎宁安 (Caitlin Cunningham) 在执掌约 11 个月后，因“失去信心”而于 9 月 27 日被解职。在周四的返校节上，三等士官杰西·布莱森第一个下船，成为“初吻”抽奖的获胜者。他和妻子阿里安娜·里奥斯站在一起，开玩笑说这次部署涉及“大量的水”。 “加入海军，看看世界——但世界 70% 都是水，”他笑着说。但是，他补充说，工作人员很棒。 “我认为你可以把这艘船上的任何人放在任何其他船上，他们都会脱颖而出，”布莱森说。 ]]>

【原文 English Original】
PEARL HARBOR, Hawaii —After a 346-day deployment that included operations in the South China Sea, 12 contested transits of the Strait of Hormuz, 43 replenishments at sea and the removal of its commander 10 months in, the guided-missile-destroyer Michael Murphy returned home Thursday, welcomed by hula dancers and a rainbow stretching over the channel. The ship was attached to the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group for much of its deployment, though the aircraft carrier returned to its home in San Diego on Oct. 8. But any deployment-length records it may have broken were short lived. The Spruance, another Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, returned home today after a 12-month deployment, and the Japan-based John Finn crew has been told to expect a 13- to 14-month deployment. As Defense One reported on Oct. 22, Navy officials have told families to expect 10- to 10-month deployments for the foreseeable future—a stark contrast from the typical 7-month deployments of recent decades. The Navy’s top enlisted sailor, Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman, confirmed that a week later, saying 10-11 months will be the norm for at least a few years. The Micheal Murphy left Hawaii on Dec. 1, 2025, and sailed through the South China Sea and Strait of Malacca before reaching the North Arabian Sea, where it spent the bulk of the deployment, said Cmdr. David Nicolas, who took command of the destroyer a month ago. The Michael Murphy launched Tomahawk missile strikes during Operation Epic Fury and took part in the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, Nicolas said. “I’m incredibly proud to be part of this team,” he said. “This is the most resilient crew that I’ve had the pleasure to serve with.” Nicolas previously commanded the Oscar Austin, another guided-missile destroyer. When he handed over the helm to his successor on Sept. 10, he was slated to become an instructor at Surface Warfare Schools in Rhode Island, according to a Navy press release . But a Navy official confirmed to Defense One that his plans were changed when the Michael Murphy’s previous boss, Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham, was relieved on Sept. 27 due to a “loss of confidence” after roughly 11 months in charge.    At Thursday’s homecoming, Petty Officer 3rd Class Jesse Bryson was first off the ship, as the winner of the “first kiss” raffle. Standing with his wife, Arianna Rios, he joked that the deployment involved “a lot of water.” “Join the Navy, see the world—but the world is 70-percent water,” he said with a laugh. But, he added, the crew was great. “I think you could put anyone from this ship on any other ship and they’d stand out,” Bryson said. ]]>

title: ‘Davidson Window’ Admiral Hopes He Was Wrong On China’s Ability To Take Taiwan By 2027
zh_title: “戴维森之窗”海军上将希望他对中国 2027 年占领台湾能力的判断是错误的
summary: 五年前，这位在国会作证的人提出了所谓的“戴维森窗口”，即中国有能力在 2027 年之前对台湾发动可信的入侵，现在这个日期即将到来，他为他的想法提供了一些见解。当时在太平洋地区指挥美军的海军上将菲利普·戴维森 (Philip Davidson) 在周五发布的播客中表示，自他 2021 年退役以来发生的一些事态发展可能会改变他的预测。然而，美国印太司令部（现太平洋司令部或PACOM）前司令告诉我们为什么要关心这个问题
content:
五年前，这位在国会作证的人提出了所谓的“戴维森窗口”，即中国有能力在 2027 年之前对台湾发动可信的入侵，现在这个日期即将到来，他为他的想法提供了一些见解。当时在太平洋地区指挥美军的海军上将菲利普·戴维森 (Philip Davidson) 在周五发布的播客中表示，自他 2021 年退役以来发生的一些事态发展可能会改变他的预测。然而，美国印太司令部（现太平洋司令部或PACOM）前司令告诉《我们为什么要关心印太？》他仍然认为有理由担心。他特别敦促美国在入侵台湾之前向台湾提供军事援助，以更好地威慑中国采取行动。中国军队练习海滩登陆。 (解放军) 戴维森发表上述声明之际，中国一直在稳步增加在台湾周边的军事演习，中国认为台湾是一个分裂的省份，有朝一日将重新置于其控制之下。在了解戴维森对 SeaLight 基金会创始人兼执行董事雷·鲍威尔 (Ray Powell) 和 BowerGroupAsia 高级顾问吉姆·卡鲁索 (Jim Carouso) 所说的话之前，让我们回顾一下戴维森于 2021 年 3 月 9 日对参议院军事委员会所说的话。
戴维森在谈到中国​​时表示：“我担心他们正在加速实现取代美国的野心，以及我们在基于规则的国际秩序中发挥领导作用的野心，他们长期以来一直表示希望在 2050 年之前实现这一目标，我担心他们会进一步接近这一目标。”菲利普·戴维森，当时担任海军上将和美国印度太平洋司令部司令。 （美国海军）两年后，对所谓“戴维森之窗”的评估得到了中央情报局（CIA）的支持。时任中央情报局局长比尔·伯恩斯 (Bill Burns) 表示：“习主席已指示中国军事领导层解放军 (PLA) 在 2027 年之前做好入侵台湾的准备。”从那以后发生了什么变化？ “从本质上讲，我希望我是错的，”戴维森在谈到他的国会证词时说道。 “如果我错了，那就意味着我们向印太司令部建议的事情、美国政府和其他国家政府在过去七年里采取的事情是有效的。而且没有发生战争。” “我主张，从军事意义上来说，五套能力——我认为很重要的投资指南，”戴维森解释道，他现在是国防承包商 AV 的董事会成员。
“美国需要重新考虑其在印太地区的兵力态势和设计——我们在哪里、我们如何部署、我们轮换什么、这些部队的能力是什么。我们还需要更多样化、更大规模的联合部队火力，这意味着进攻性火力不仅来自海上，还来自陆地和空中。”这位海军上将补充道：“你现在肯定会看到这种情况正在发生，包括部署和导弹部署、海军陆战队、陆军在菲律宾和第一岛链沿线的部署。” “这很有帮助。”第 1 多域特遣部队远程火力营第 3 野战炮兵团第 5 营查理炮台的中程能力 (MRC) 发射器抵达菲律宾吕宋岛北部战区，这是该能力首次部署到战区的一部分

The man whose congressional testimony five years ago led to what’s known as the “Davidson Window” for China being capable of launching a credible invasion of Taiwan by 2027 is offering some insights into what he is thinking now that the date is drawing near. Philip Davidson – the admiral who led U.S. forces in the Pacific at the time – said on a podcast released Friday that several developments have taken place since he retired in 2021 that could change his projection. However, the former commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command (now Pacific Command or PACOM) told the Why Should We Care About the Indo-Pacific? podcast he still sees reasons for concern. In particular, he urged the U.S. to deliver military aid to Taiwan before an invasion to better deter China from acting. Chinese forces practice a beach landing. (PLA) Davidson’s statements were delivered as China has been steadily increasing military exercises around Taiwan , which it considers a breakaway province that it will someday bring back under its control. Before getting into what Davidson told podcasters Ray Powell, founder and executive director of the SeaLight Foundation , and Jim Carouso, a senior advisor at BowerGroupAsia , let’s recall what Davidson told the Senate Armed Services Committee on March 9, 2021. “I worry that they are accelerating their ambitions to supplant the United States, and our leadership role in the rules-based international order, which they have long said that they want to do that by 2050, I am worried about them moving that target closer,” Davidson said of China. “Taiwan is clearly one of their ambitions before then, and I think the threat is manifest during this decade, in fact, in the next six years.” Philip Davidson when he was a Navy admiral and commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command. (USN) The assessment of the so-called “Davidson Window” was backed two years later by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). “President Xi has instructed the PLA [People’s Liberation Army], the Chinese military leadership, to be ready by 2027 to invade Taiwan,” then-CIA Director Bill Burns stated . What’s Changed Since Then? “At the heart of it, I’m hoping to be wrong,” said Davidson about his congressional testimony. “If I’m wrong, that means the things we recommended from Indo-Pacific Command, the things that the United States government and other governments have undertaken over the last seven years, have been effective. And there hasn’t been war.” “I advocated for, just in the military sense, five capability sets – investment guidelines that I thought were important to do,” explained Davidson, now on the board of directors at defense contractor AV . “The United States needed to rethink its force posture and design in the region, in the Indo-Pacific – where we are, how we deployed, what we rotated through, what the capabilities of those sets were. We also needed more diverse and a larger set of joint force fires, meaning offensive fires, not just from the sea, but from land and air domain.” “You’re certainly seeing that play out right now, with deployments and missile deployments, with Marine formations , Army formations in the Philippines and along the First Island Chain,” the admiral added. “That has been a help.” Mid-Range Capability (MRC) Launcher from Charlie Battery, 5th Battalion, 3rd Field Artillery Regiment, Long Range Fires Battalion, 1st Multi-Domain Task Force arrives as part of the capability’s first deployment into theater on Northern Luzon, Philippines, April 8, 2024. The MRC deployment aims to enhance Philippine maritime defense capabilities, while bolstering interoperability and readiness within the U.S.-Philippine Alliance. (U.S. Army) U.S. Army In addition, Davidson noted that the U.S. “needed to improve our exercises, our experimentation, and our innovation in the region. We have deepened the relationship with Japan and Australia in the Keen series of exercises over the last five years, and in a way that was kind of unheard of in my day, which I think is a profound improvement.” The Keen Sword training exercise occurred last month and saw about “45,000 Japan Self-Defense Force, 11,000 U.S. service members and forces from Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines…participating alongside observers from the Republic of Korea and the United Kingdom,” according to the U.S. Navy. A Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force Landing Craft Air Cushion (LCAC) hovercraft assigned to Amphibious Warfare Squadron One, Amphibious and Mine Warfare Group, coasts into the harbor at Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni, Japan, Oct. 28, 2026, during Keen Sword. (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Donald Dugger) Lance Cpl. Donald Dugger Japan taking a more assertive security posture toward China has been a huge change from when he was in command, Davidson noted. “Japan absolutely has come forward, they reissued their national security strategy in December of [2022], and there were a number of alliance announcements made in January of [2023],” he explained.  The Japanese doubled their investment in defense from 1% to 2% of its GDP, Davidson highlighted. Japan also “established space [and] cyber forces, instilled the cybersecurity principles and laws that would be necessary to deepen our relationship in a classified way. And this is almost unknown to anybody in America. Completely redistributed and reset their ground formations and air formations in the Southwest Island chain, between Okinawa and along the Ryukyu chain.” “Most importantly, they identified China as the strategic threat in the region,” Davidson proffered. “And in the alliance announcement in January of [2023] with us, said that our interests have converged in this regard.” A Japan Air Self-Defense Force F-15 fighter performs during the Komatsu Air Festival on September 26, 2026 in Komatsu, Japan. (Photo by Zhang Hui/VCG via Getty Images) VCG Taiwan too has made some needed improvements in its approach to defending itself since he retired, Davidson explained. “You have to be encouraged by Taiwan’s actions taken since then,” he stated. “They expanded the conscription timeline from just a few months to a year of service. They have done an enormous amount of work in their national emergency preparedness realm.” Davidson also credited Adm. Lee Hsi-min, chief of the Taiwanese Armed Forces general staff from 2017 to 2019, for developing the Overall Defense Concept (ODC). Lee envisioned a mix of mines, uncrewed aerial systems (UAS), uncrewed surface vehicles (USVs), uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs), crewed coastal defense boats, land-based mobile short- and medium-range precision munitions, precision-guided multiple launch rocket systems, man portable air defense systems (MANPADS), anti-armor rocket systems and electronic warfare measures to counter the PLA’s overwhelming advantages in aviation and naval assets and long-range fires. Taiwan sits about 130 miles east of China. (Google Earth) “He said, ‘We really have to develop the kind of asymmetric capabilities that help round out our lack of capacity vis-a-vis its relationship with the People’s Republic of China, and make sure that we have a strategic and operational design that can kill in the littoral and along the landing beaches and things like that,’” Davidson pointed out. “They’ve been getting after autonomy. They’ve been getting after robotics and drones and sensing.” In 2025, Taiwan revealed a new drone boat, or uncrewed surface vessel (USV), the Endeavor Manta, said to be the first of its kind for the Republic of China Navy (ROCN). However, as we have frequently pointed out , Taiwan is still far behind where it needs to be in many of these areas, but especially uncrewed systems . In addition, Davidson said growing relations with the Philippines and Australia are also helping. Australia signed the Australia–United Kingdom–United States security partnership (AUKUS) in September 2021, months after Davidson retired. AUKUS calls for the United States and Britain to share nuclear-submarine technology with Australia. A rendering of the future SSN-AUKUS design. (U.K. Ministry of Defense) “So over the span of the last six years since March 9 of 2021, you’ve seen a lot of change that I think has reinforced the deterrence of the West here, and I think that’s important to note,” Davidson stated. What Still Needs To Change Despite seeing the U.S. and its allies better prepared to defend against a Chinese invasion of Taiwan, Davidson said he is concerned that the U.S. is not moving fast enough to provide promised military aid. “I would like to see the $14 billion in committed [Foreign Military Sales] to Taiwan move over there in the next few months or a year,” Davidson stated. Approval of the package, which is a major point of controversy with China, has been stalled, Taiwan’s Defense Minister Wellington Koo said in September . The minister’s remarks “come as concerns mount that President Donald Trump could halt arms sales to Taiwan. China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a May summit in Beijing between Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping,” The Associated Press noted . “The United States paused the $14 billion arms deal after that meeting.” The package “largely consists of [Patriot] PAC-3 and NASAMS [ National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System ] air defense missiles,” Reuters reported . However, another huge factor beyond tensions with China is the U.S. supply of these air defense munitions, which has been drastically affected by the current and recent Middle East conflicts . Donations to Ukraine have also eaten into U.S. stocks. The lack of sufficient magazine depth is an issue that TWZ has raised frequently for years, and especially in regard to America’s air and missile defenses , in particular. Commitments for deliveries to 20 other nations and an overall insatiable global demand for interceptors due to numerous destabilizing events has put further strain on the supply of American interceptors. All this is also straining the ability of industry to provide enough capacity. For instance, current PAC-3 MSE production “is around the baseline rate of 650 interceptors per year, with half the deliveries going to the United States and the rest to allies and partners,” according to a report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). The Pentagon is trying to boost production. Under a contract with the Pentagon inked in January , Lockheed Martin is committed to raising annual Patriot output to 2,000 interceptors. A Patriot PAC-3 interceptor (Lockheed Martin) In addition to wanting to see the arms package pushed forward, Davidson warned about China’s information warfare capabilities. “The one thing that has really jumped out at me that was a problem, certainly, when I was the Indo-Pacific commander, but it’s worse now, is the information environment,” Davidson posited. “China is working to undermine the democratic processes in Taiwan. They’re working to undermine any U.S. citizens’ confidence in business leadership and political leadership and military leadership. They’re exploiting accidents or difficulties that someone might be having to flood social networks, and it’s happening not just from China, but from Russia and Iran and independent actors elsewhere. “ “It’s really dangerous,” the former commander emphasized. “There’s been some estimations that some of the activity from bots and from propaganda players is accounting for up to 70% of the commentary in social media threads here and there, and that’s a much more difficult place to be.” Davidson said the U.S. needs to step up its own information warfare capabilities. “I think we should be putting as much effort into [the information domain] as we’ve been putting into drones and autonomy and things like that in this day and age,” Davidson stated. Chinese hovercraft land on a beach during training. (PLAN) Davidson did not address some other glaring issues in regard to China’s potential seizure of Taiwan. The biggest being will the U.S. actually respond militarily if a major Chinese exercise suddenly became an actual invasion operation? Would there even be enough time and what about China’s anti-access capabilities that could keep much of America’s combat power at bay during the early stages of such a conflict? Would there even be support for such an intervention operation domestically, especially considering it could be very bloody and it would surely manifest itself here at home? Then, as we mentioned in the piece, there are many areas where Taiwan seems to be moving far too slowly while China’s military force continues to balloon on nearly all fronts. Regardless, it’s nice to hear from the man who inadvertently gave birth to the “Davidson Window” now that this ominous window of vulnerability he predicted a half decade is cracking open. content:
TWZ 获得了有关海狼级潜艇康涅狄格号在 2021 年在南中国海与水下海山相撞后正在进行维修的新细节。海军一直在考虑大约三年的时间表来建造替换的船首声纳导流罩。最终，仅用了不到一年的时间就建成了。康涅狄格州的总体维修计划已被推迟，我们是第一个报告该船预计要到明年夏天才能恢复使用的人。编者注：这篇报道发表后，Janicki Industries 联系我们，要求在进行额外审查时删除圆顶的图像。出于礼貌，我们同意了，如果完全获得批准，我们将重新发布它。 Janicki Industries 今天告诉我们，该公司在大约 10 个月内生产出了新型船首声纳导流罩，并于 2024 年交付给海军。据其网站称，Janicki 拥有为美国核潜艇项目生产“声纳罩和精密加工硬件”的历史。它还支持各种备受瞩目的航空航天项目，包括 B-21 袭击者轰炸机和 F-35 联合攻击战斗机。根据一份经过大量编辑的海军事故报告，康涅狄格号的船头在五年前的碰撞事件发生后，最初至少在某种程度上仍然保持着连接状态。然而，当潜艇一瘸一拐地驶向关岛时，整个船首结构随后断裂。
随后，这艘船驶往加利福尼亚州圣地亚哥，然后前往华盛顿州的普吉特海湾海军造船厂和中间维护设施 (PSNS-IMF)，此后一直待在那里。 2023 年，在普吉特湾海军造船厂和中间维护设施中看到的康涅狄格号航空母舰，其船首圆顶明显缺失。美国海军“普吉特海湾海军造船厂和国际货币基金组织（中间维护设施）需要按照船的计划，在其后面没有生产线的情况下安装一个精密的替换圆顶，”贾尼基在撰写本文时还在其网站上表示。 “Janicki 比次佳选择快了 24 个月，因为工作所需的一切都集中在一个屋檐下：适合半球的 5 轴铣床、证明这一点的计量方法以及形成双曲板的 1,000 吨压力机。”本文顶部的部分图片和下面的完整图片显示了 Janicki 专有的五轴铣床在圆顶上工作的情况。海狼级潜艇艏声纳导流罩的尺寸和复杂性怎么强调都不为过。这些船上的船首声纳阵列直径为 24 英尺。圆顶本身的结构必须按照非常严格的规格建造，以使声纳系统正常工作。海狼级潜艇上的艏声纳阵列，其艏穹顶被拆除。公共领域 过去的五角大楼预算文件和国会拨款法案已经强调了更换康涅狄格州弓形声纳罩的预期成本和复杂性。
2021 年，立法者批准了 1000 万美元专门用于圆顶的资金，以及 4000 万美元用于其他“紧急维修”。全部维修费用仍不得而知，但预计将远高于 5000 万美元。 在 2024 年发布的 2025 财年预算提案中，海军还概述了购买额外船首圆顶的计划，以防其任何一艘“海狼”级潜艇再次遭受类似的严重事故。 “海狼级潜艇的保障战略不包括提供替换潜艇

【原文 English Original】
TWZ has obtained new details about the ongoing repairs to the Seawolf class submarine USS Connecticut following collision with an underwater seamount in the South China Sea in 2021. The Navy had been looking at a roughly three-year timeline for the construction of a replacement bow sonar dome. In the end, it took just under a year for it to be built. The overall schedule for repairs to Connecticut has suffered delays, and we were the first to report that the boat is now not expected to return to service until next summer. Editor’s note: After this story was published, Janicki Industries reached out to us to ask that the image of the dome be taken down while an additional review is conducted. Out of courtesy, we agreed, and we will repost it if and when it is fully approved. Janicki Industries produced the new bow sonar dome in approximately 10 months and delivered it to the Navy in 2024, the company told us today. Janicki has a history of producing “sonar domes and precision machined hardware” for U.S. nuclear submarine programs, according to its website . It has also supported various high-profile aerospace programs, including the B-21 Raider bomber and F-35 Joint Strike Fighter . Connecticut ’s bow had initially remained attached, at least to some degree, following the collision five years ago, according to a heavily redacted Navy report on the accident . However, the entire bow structure subsequently broke away as the submarine limped to Guam . The boat then sailed to San Diego, California , and then to the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance Facility (PSNS-IMF) in Washington State, where it has been ever since. USS Connecticut seen at the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance Facility in 2023 with its bow dome prominently missing. USN “Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & IMF [Intermediate Maintenance Facility] needed a precision replacement dome with no production line behind it, on the boat’s schedule,” Janicki also says on its website at the time of writing . “Janicki delivered it 24 months faster than the next-best option because everything the job needed sits under one roof: 5-axis mills that fit a hemisphere, the metrology to prove it, and the 1,000-ton press that forms double-curved plate.” The picture seen in part at the top of this story and in full below shows one of Janicki’s proprietary five-axis milling machines at work on the dome. The size and complexity of the bow sonar dome on Seawolf class submarines cannot be overstated. The bow sonar arrays on these boats is 24 feet in diameter. The structure of the dome itself has to be built to very exacting specifications for the sonar system to work properly. A look at the bow sonar array on a Seawolf class submarine with its bow dome removed. Public Domain Past Pentagon budget documents and appropriations bills from Congress had already highlighted the expected costs and complexities of replacing Connecticut ’s bow sonar dome. In 2021, lawmakers approved $10 million in funding specifically for the dome, as well as $40 million for other “emergent repairs.” The full repair bill is still unknown, but is expected to be far steeper than just $50 million. In its Fiscal Year 2025 budget proposal , released in 2024, the Navy also outlined plans to acquire an additional bow dome in case any of its Seawolf class submarines suffered another similarly severe mishap. “The Seawolf Class submarines sustainment strategy did not include the provisioning of replacement bow domes; therefore, no replacement bow domes for these in-service submarines are within the Navy’s inventory,” the budget documents explained. “This program would procure one Seawolf Class bow dome for use in the event replacement is required. Funds in FY25 are to purchase a bow dome which has a three plus year lead time.” Note here the mention of a lead time of at least three years, which is in line with Janicki’s statement that the “next-best option” would have taken two years more to do this work. As TWZ has highlighted in years of reporting now, repairs to Connecticut , in general, were always set to be challenging and costly due to the small size of the Seawolf class and the design being long out of production. The Navy originally planned to acquire 29 of these boats, but ultimately bought just three as a result of post-Cold War drawdowns. In addition, shrinking the program of record so severely caused the unit price of each one to rise substantially, just over $10 billion in 2025 dollars. At the time of writing, they are still the most costly attack submarines ever built. The last of the Seawolf class submarines, the highly secretive USS Jimmy Carter , which entered service in 2005, is also a heavily modified sub-type optimized for underwater espionage missions . USS Connecticut at sea in 2009. USN It is also worth noting that the U.S. Navy, as well as some of its foreign counterparts , have repaired similarly severe damage to submarines by cannibalizing entire sections from decommissioned boats in the same class. However, this is not an option given the size of the Seawolf class and the still very high demand for them operationally . The core design offers advanced capabilities that make even USS Seawolf and USS Connecticut especially well suited to a variety of specialized tasks . This is clearly why the Navy has continued to invest so much in returning Connecticut to the fleet. As mentioned, repairs to Connecticut are now not expected to be finished until sometime in the summer of next year. This is the latest in a succession of schedule slips in recent years. The original goal had been for the boat to be back in service by September 2025. “The Navy’s target completion date for the availability is the summer of 2027. PSNS & IMF is dedicated to executing this work with the highest standards of safety, technical accuracy, and craftsmanship to ensure the ship returns to the fleet ready to take its place at the tip of the spear in defense of our nation’s interests,” a Navy official told TWZ in September. “Current work consists of structural and systems restoration and required lifecycle maintenance.” Earlier in the year, the Navy also revealed that it is now planning on sending Connecticut into retirement in 2031. This means the submarine has just four more years of service ahead of it if the current repair schedule holds. The Navy does have plans to acquire a new class of nuclear attack submarines, currently referred to as SSN(X). In the past, the service has described those future boats as more of a direct successor to the Seawolf class than the versions of the Virginia class it is buying now. A picture of the first-in-class USS Seawolf . USN “The analytical conclusion was unequivocal: to dominate high-end peer threats in the middle of this century, a clean sheet design is required. The Virginia class is a fantastic, unmatched world-class warship, and it will remain the backbone of our attack fleet for decades,” Navy Rear Adm. Andrew Miller said at the Naval Submarine League’s main annual conference last week, per USNI News . “As adversary capabilities evolve, we require expanded payload capacity, greater electrical and hydrodynamic margins and unprecedented architectural flexibility that simply cannot be backfitted into an existing hull form.” Miller is currently the head of the Undersea Warfare Division with the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations. In terms of desired key capabilities for SSN(X), the Navy wants “first, higher flank speed and tactical control speed. Two, improved operational availability. Three, decisive lethality. Four, superior stealth and layered survivability, and finally organic robotic and autonomous systems hosting and command and control,” Miller added. “We are redefining the role of the submarine from a standalone hunter-killer to a capital mothership. By launching uncrewed systems directly from submarine torpedo tubes and integrating unmanned [robotic] vehicles into our battle plans, we dramatically expand the tactical reach of our manned fleet.” The first SSN(X) submarines are not expected to begin entering service until the mid-2040s, at the earliest. The Navy will continue acquiring Virginia class submarines in the interim. This includes stretched Block IV and V versions with Virginia Payload Modules (VPM) that will now be categorized as guided-missile types (SSGN). There will also be a one-of-a-kind seabed warfare version of the Virginia , which could well take over for the USS Jimmy Carter. A briefing slide from General Dynamics Electric Boat detailing existing and future planned subvariants of the Virginia class nuclear submarine. The Block VI and V types have now been reclassified as nuclear-powered guided missile submarines (SSGN) rather than nuclear-powered attack submarines (SSN). General Dynamics Electric Boat When it comes to USS Connecticut , if there are no further delays, the fully repaired submarine with its new bow sonar dome should be back in service by the middle of next year. WASHINGTON — Space tracking firm LeoLabs [today announced](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/leolabs-acquires-fisheye-to-accelerate-delivery-of-next-generation-radars-optimized-for-missile-warning-and-tracking-302939602.html) it has acquired FishEye Software as it looks to expand its missile defense footprint.

“As a wholly owned subsidiary of LeoLabs, FishEye will strengthen our ability to accelerate delivery of our next-generation radars optimized for missile warning and tracking, such as [Scout-X](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/09/shifting-market-sands-leolabs-moves-to-sell-new-mobile-space-radar-directly-to-allies/),” a LeoLabs spokesperson told Breaking Defense.

The highly mobile Scout-X made its debut[in June](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/06/leolabs-new-mobile-space-watch-radar-to-participate-in-valiant-shield-exercise/)during during US Indo-Pacific Command’s multinational Valiant Shield exercise. The radar fits in a standard shipping container and can detect both satellites and missiles flying at altitudes of about 230 to 1,000 kilometers (143 miles to 621 miles) above the Earth.

Founded in 1997 and headquartered in Massachusetts, FishEye has a pedigree in supporting the Pentagon’s missile defense programs. It is one of several thousand small firms chosen [last December](https://breakingdefense.com/2025/12/mda-picks-over-1000-initial-winners-for-golden-dome-contracting-vehicle/) for the Missile Defense Agency’s Scalable Homeland Innovative Enterprise Layered Defense ([SHIELD](https://breakingdefense.com/2025/08/mda-outlines-golden-domes-shield-151-billion-contracting-vehicle/))contract vehicle, which is worth up to $151 billion through 2035,and supports the Trump administration’s [Golden Dome](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/golden-dome/) initiative.

“FishEye brings decades of experience developing and integrating software for U.S. missile defense systems,” LeoLabs CEO Tony Frazier said in a statement. “That expertise will help us continue to adapt our proven radar technology for missile warning and tracking, and move those capabilities into operational use quickly.”

While the LeoLabs announcement did not reveal the price tag of the acquisition, FishEye’s revenue is projected to reach approximately $11.9 million this year, according to corporate research website [RocketReach.](https://rocketreach.co/fisheye-software-inc-profile_b5c759b1f42e0d08)

zh_title: 东北亚空中警报频发后，俄罗斯Tu-95轰炸机抵达越南
summary: 俄罗斯派遣两架Tu-95MS“熊”轰炸机罕见地访问越南。不同寻常的是，这架飞机似乎短暂侵入日本领空，并沿途穿过台湾防空识别区（ADIZ）。此次活动距离中国国家主席习近平、俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京和美国总统唐纳德·特朗普将在中国深圳举行史无前例的三边会议仅48小时。一段视频的屏幕截图显示，Tu-95MS 飞行员于 2026 年 1 月 21 日在日本海上空进行了一次飞行。照片由 Russian Defence Min 摄
content:
俄罗斯派遣两架Tu-95MS“熊”轰炸机罕见地访问越南。不同寻常的是，这架飞机似乎短暂侵入日本领空，并沿途穿过台湾防空识别区（ADIZ）。此次活动距离中国国家主席习近平、俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京和美国总统唐纳德·特朗普将在中国深圳举行史无前例的三边会议仅48小时。一段视频的屏幕截图显示，2026 年 1 月 21 日，一架 Tu-95MS 的飞行员在前一次飞越日本海时。照片由俄罗斯国防部/阿纳多卢通过 Getty Images 拍摄 Anadolu 11 月 16 日至 17 日，Tu-95MS 轰炸机是几架俄罗斯军用飞机之一，在东北亚进行了广泛的演习，引发了三个地区政府的防空反应。据分析师 AviVector 称，共有五架涡轮螺旋桨动力轰炸机于 11 月 16 日从俄罗斯远东的乌克兰基地起飞。据报道，其中三架轰炸机在三架 Il-78M Midas 空中加油机的支援下，在日本海上空进行了大约 11 小时的训练飞行。据报道，一架 A-50U Mainstay 空中预警和控制飞机也在日本海上空飞行。与此同时，另外两架 Tu-95MS 继续向南驶向越南。今天，乌克兰空军基地的三架 Tu-95MS 和三架 Il-78M 在日本海上空进行了 11 小时的训练飞行。
一架 A-50U（RF-94268，红色 41）从符拉迪沃斯托克机场起飞，在日本海上空进行了一次侦察飞行。两架 Tu-95MS（RF-94202，红色 43；RF-94188，红色 44）… https://t.co/ezIP4s4mxl pic.twitter.com/9fvc2QZsFC — AviVector (@avivector) 11 月 17 日， 2026 日本和台湾均未正式确定参与各自空域事件的飞机类型。日本防卫省证实，11 月 17 日早些时候，两架据信是俄罗斯的飞机侵犯了福冈县冲之岛西北部的领空。第一架飞机于当地时间凌晨 4 点 07 分左右进入，于凌晨 4 点 10 分起飞。第二架飞机于凌晨 4 点 09 分左右进入，于 2026 年 4 月 10 日起飞。据日本防卫省称，凌晨 4 点 12 分，日本认为俄罗斯飞机于 11 月 17 日早些时候进入福冈附近冲之岛西北部的日本领空，第一架飞机于当地时间凌晨 4 点 07 分至 4 点 10 分左右进入日本领空，第二架飞机于当地时间凌晨 4 点 09 分至 4 点 12 分左右进入日本… https://t.co/Sj7vHUFDMQ pic.twitter.com/wYbdE7GWTH — 台湾安全监察站 (@TaiwanMonitor) 2026 年 11 月 17 日，日本防卫省称，日本航空自卫队 (JASDF) 紧急出动西方防空部队的战斗机，发出警告并采取其他措施。
穿过对马海峡后，飞机在与那国岛和台湾之间飞行，然后继续进入太平洋。 2026年11月17日，推测的俄罗斯飞机的飞行路线。 日本联合参谋部 该航线使飞机经过连接日本海、东海和西太平洋的几个具有重要战略意义的海上通道。据报道，俄罗斯飞机随后进入韩国防空识别区（KADIZ）。不过，据韩国国防部称，此次事件并未侵犯韩国领空。

【原文 English Original】
Russia has sent a pair of Tu-95MS Bear bombers for a rare visit to Vietnam. Unusually, the aircraft appear to have briefly intruded into Japanese airspace and passed through Taiwan’s Air Defense Identification Zone (ADIZ) along the way. The activity unfolded just 48 hours before Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and U.S. President Donald Trump are due to hold an unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China. A screen grab from a video shows the pilot of a Tu-95MS during a previous flight over the Sea of Japan on January 21, 2026. Photo by Russian Defense Ministry/Anadolu via Getty Images Anadolu The Tu-95MS bombers were among several Russian military aircraft conducting extensive maneuvers across Northeast Asia on November 16-17, prompting air defense responses from three regional governments. According to analyst AviVector , a total of five of the turboprop-powered bombers departed their home base of Ukrainka in Russia’s Far East on November 16. Three of the bombers reportedly conducted an approximately 11-hour training flight over the Sea of Japan, supported by three Il-78M Midas aerial refueling tankers. An A-50U Mainstay airborne early warning and control aircraft was also reported operating over the Sea of Japan. Meanwhile, the other two Tu-95MS continued south towards Vietnam. Today, three Tu-95MS and three Il-78M from Ukrainka Air Base conducted an 11-hour training flight over the Sea of Japan. An A-50U (RF-94268, 41 Red) from Vladivostok Airport conducted a reconnaissance flight over the Sea of Japan. Two Tu-95MS (RF-94202, 43 Red; RF-94188, 44… https://t.co/ezIP4s4mxl pic.twitter.com/9fvc2QZsFC — AviVector (@avivector) November 17, 2026 Neither Japan nor Taiwan officially identified the aircraft types involved in their respective airspace incidents. Japan’s Ministry of Defense confirmed that two separate aircraft believed to be Russian violated its territorial airspace northwest of Okinoshima, in Fukuoka Prefecture, early on November 17. The first aircraft entered at approximately 4:07 a.m. local time and departed at 4:10 a.m. A second aircraft entered at approximately 4:09 a.m. and departed at 4:12 a.m. Two aircraft Japan believes are Russian entered Japanese territorial airspace northwest of Okinoshima, off Fukuoka, early Nov. 17, per Japan's Ministry of Defense. The first was inside from about 4:07 to 4:10 a.m. local time and the second from about 4:09 to 4:12 a.m. The Japan… https://t.co/Sj7vHUFDMQ pic.twitter.com/wYbdE7GWTH — Taiwan Security Monitor (台灣安全觀測站) (@TaiwanMonitor) November 17, 2026 The Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) scrambled fighters from its Western Air Defense Force to issue warnings and take other measures, according to the country’s Ministry of Defense. Tokyo subsequently lodged what it described as a strong protest with Moscow over the incident. Japan also provided details of the aircraft’s subsequent route. After passing through the Tsushima Strait , the planes flew between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan before continuing into the Pacific Ocean. Flight path of the presumed Russian aircraft on November 17, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office The route placed the aircraft through several strategically important maritime approaches connecting the Sea of Japan , East China Sea , and western Pacific. The Russian aircraft then reportedly entered South Korea’s Air Defense Identification Zone (KADIZ). However, there was no violation of South Korean airspace, according to the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff. Finally, Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense reported detecting two Russian military aircraft entering its ADIZ from the northeast. Overall, 2 sorties of Russian military aircraft were detected early this morning. The aircraft entered #Taiwan 's ADIZ from the northeast, flew through airspace east of Taiwan, and exited the ADIZ south of Taitung. The #ROCArmedForces have monitored the situation and responded… — 國防部 Ministry of National Defense, ROC(Taiwan) (@MoNDefense) November 17, 2026 The aircraft proceeded through airspace east of Taiwan before exiting south of Taitung. Taiwan’s armed forces monitored the activity and responded accordingly, the Ministry of National Defense said. The incident is notable because Taiwan’s defence ministry publicly identified the aircraft as Russian, rather than simply reporting unidentified military aircraft activity. As we have reported in the past , Chinese aircraft commonly fly into the southwestern part of Taiwan’s ADIZ. It is, however, worth noting that the ADIZ declared by Taiwan covers not only the entirety of the Strait but also portions of mainland China. In terms of Russian aircraft operating in Taiwan’s ADIZ, there are historical precedents, but such activity has been greatly reduced since the end of the Cold War. Taiwanese military analyst Chieh Chung told Focus Taiwan that Soviet and Russian military aircraft had previously operated inside Taiwan’s ADIZ in 1986 and January 2010. "The incident was not the first time Russian or former Soviet military aircraft had entered Taiwan's ADIZ, although such flights have become much less frequent since the end of the Cold War." https://t.co/TPUJL9hfp1 https://t.co/SDB6p3E3pD — Bryce C. Barros 白若詩 (@barros_bryce) November 17, 2026 The two remaining Tu-95MS aircraft continued south towards Vietnam and were subsequently reported at Da Nang on November 17. They were accompanied by a pair of Il-76MD Candid transports, one of which was a modernized -90A variant , to support the deployment. Tu-95MS strategic missile carriers RF-94202, RF-94188. Il-76MD, Da Nang Airport / "Danang 35K Feet". pic.twitter.com/22DaoD8PLP — Massimo Frantarelli (@MrFrantarelli) November 17, 2026 [Russie Vietnam] 2 Tu-95MS des forces aérospatiales russes sont arrivés à l'aéroport international de Da Nang (DAD/VVDN), au Vietnam. 2 avions de transport militaire IL-76 (MD et MD-90A) les accompagnaient. (c) AviaNews pic.twitter.com/4bWfFXFOik — La souris (@La_souris_DA) November 17, 2026 The flights took place against the backdrop of preparations for the November 19 meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin in China. The summit is set to be held on the sidelines of meetings of the  Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), which kick off tomorrow. Putin arrived in Shenzhen today. Trump has traveled first to the Philippines as part of a short tour of Asia before heading to China. Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen in the early hours of Nov. 18 to attend the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting. ： @PDChina pic.twitter.com/5YotpjYY6R — Shenzhen Daily (@szdaily1) November 17, 2026 The proximity of the Russian operation to the Shenzhen meeting raises questions about the strategic signaling of the Russian flights, particularly as the three governments prepare to discuss nuclear arms control, regional security, and other major international issues. The meeting is particularly unusual given the different priorities each leader is bringing to the table . Trump has indicated that he wants to discuss reducing nuclear arsenals and addressing the war in Iran. The expiration of the New START treaty in February 2026 removed the remaining bilateral limits on U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear forces, adding urgency to the question of future arms-control arrangements. U.S. President Barack Obama, at left, and Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, at right, shake hands after signing the New START treaty in 2010. Government of Russia Washington has tempered expectations of an immediate agreement, describing the gathering as an initial opportunity for the three nuclear powers to begin a conversation. Putin, meanwhile, is expected to seek discussion of Russia’s war against Ukraine and the possibility of a negotiated settlement. Moscow has signalled that Ukraine will remain a priority in its discussions with Washington. Beijing’s position is more cautious. China has resisted joining trilateral nuclear arms-control negotiations at this stage, arguing that its nuclear arsenal remains substantially smaller than those of the United States and Russia. Xi is also seeking to present China as a central diplomatic actor capable of facilitating dialogue between the other two powers. An apparent new field of Chinese intercontinental ballistic missile silos identified by Matt Korda and Hans Kristensen from the Federation of American Scientists (FAS) and located near the city of Hami in the eastern end of Xinjiang province, in the northwest of China. Kristensen/Korda/FAS 2021 The timing of the Russian aviation activity is therefore difficult to ignore. The operation demonstrated the geographic reach of Russian long-range aviation, with aircraft moving from Russia’s Far East through the approaches to Japan and Taiwan before continuing towards Vietnam. The Southeast Asian nation was a regular late Cold War operating location for Soviet naval Tu-95 Bear reconnaissance aircraft. Of course, as well as strategic signalling, flights of this kind provide valuable long-range training and intelligence collection, including assessment of regional air defense responses. The November 19 meeting may not produce an agreement on nuclear weapons or other major disputes. Still, the Russian flights underscore the fact that strategic stability in the Indo-Pacific also involves the security concerns of the regional states operating along the approaches to the western Pacific. 四方领导人峰会 联合新闻稿 搜索 选择类别 所有新闻简报和声明 所有总统行动 行政命令 提名和任命 总统备忘录公告情况说明书 发布评论 研究 所有简报和声明 总统行动 所有行政命令 提名和任命 总统备忘录公告情况说明书 发布评论 研究 2026 年 11 月 17 日 — 美国总统唐纳德·J·特朗普，总理澳大利亚部长安东尼·阿尔巴内塞、印度总理纳伦德拉·莫迪和日本首相早苗高市在马尼拉举行四方领导人峰会。今年是四方机制重启近十年，也是已故日本首相安倍晋三于 2016 年首次提出自由开放的印太愿景十周年。十年过去了，这一愿景比以往任何时候都更加强烈。我们共同证明了四方机制是一股正义力量和行动伙伴关系，致力于和平、稳定与繁荣。我们强烈反对任何试图改变现状的破坏稳定或单方面行动，包括通过武力或胁迫手段，这会导致紧张局势升级，破坏地区和平与稳定。我们对经济胁迫表示严重关切，包括任意出口限制。
我们正在确保关键供应链的安全，保护航行和飞越自由，通过未来技术推动增长，包括投资和部署值得信赖的超级智能（SI）*，并通过救生援助应对灾难。我们承诺共同努力，确保印太地区开放、安全和有弹性的海上过境走廊。我们正在与区域伙伴合作，应对共同的挑战并创造机遇，为印太地区带来切实的利益。我们宣布首届四方商界领袖论坛将于 2027 年初举行，来自四方国家的商界领袖、政府官员和政策专家将齐聚一堂，以促进私营部门之间更紧密的商业联系，包括促进对印太地区繁荣至关重要的商业交易和伙伴关系。我们肯定我们的外交部长在亚特兰大宣布的超级情报*加速器的重要性。该加速器旨在协调和资助支持可信超级情报（SI）*在整个印度-太平洋地区的访问、部署和技术援助的努力。我们很自豪地欢迎印度-太平洋海上监视合作，这是一项旨在加强信息共享和海域意识的新举措。 2027年，我们各自的P-8和P-3C巡逻机计划首次在四方背景下进行海上演习，使我们的海洋更加安全。
我们对“电缆连通性和复原力四方伙伴关系”所取得的进展感到自豪，该伙伴关系扩大了整个印度-太平洋地区安全、可信的通信基础设施的覆盖范围。今天，我们欢迎澳大利亚扩大对该伙伴关系的贡献，重点关注电缆，加强区域能源安全和连通性。我们还欢迎即将在印度洋开展的海底电缆项目，这些项目旨在加强区域互联互通。我们承认该地区网络事件的数量和规模迅速增加，并宣布加强四方网络安全合作，我们计划通过该合作共同努力

Quad Leaders’ Summit Joint Press Release Search Select Category All News Briefings & Statements All Presidential Actions Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research All Briefings & Statements Presidential Actions All Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research On November 17, 2026 — President Donald J. Trump of the United States, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of Australia, Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, and Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae of Japan — met for a Quad Leaders’ Summit in Manila. This year marks nearly a decade since the Quad was revived and the tenth anniversary of the vision of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific, first articulated by the late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo of Japan in 2016. A decade on, that vision is stronger than ever. Together, we have shown that the Quad is a force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability, and prosperity. We strongly oppose any destabilizing or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability. We express grave concerns about economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions. We are securing critical supply chains, protecting freedom of navigation and overflight, driving growth through technologies of the future including investments in and deployment of trusted Super Intelligence (SI)*, and responding to disasters with life-saving assistance. We commit to work together to ensure open, safe, and resilient maritime transit corridors in the Indo-Pacific. We are working with regional partners to tackle shared challenges and drive opportunities to deliver tangible benefits to the Indo-Pacific. We announce the inaugural Quad Business Leaders’ Forum which is scheduled to be held in early 2027, bringing together business leaders, government officials, and policy experts from Quad countries to foster greater business ties across our private sectors, including the promotion of commercial deals and partnerships critical to the prosperity of the Indo-Pacific. We affirm the importance of the Super Intelligence* Accelerator , announced by our Foreign Ministers in Atlanta.  The Accelerator is intended to coordinate and fund efforts to support trusted Super Intelligence (SI)* access, deployment, and technical assistance across the Indo-Pacific. We are proud to welcome the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration , a new initiative to enhance information sharing and maritime domain awareness.  In 2027, our respective P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft are scheduled to fly in a maritime exercise for the first time in a Quad context, making our seas safer. We are proud of progress under the Quad Partnership for Cable Connectivity and Resilience , which has expanded access to secure and trusted communications infrastructure across the Indo-Pacific.  Today, we welcome an expansion of Australia’s contribution to the Partnership to focus on electricity cables, strengthening regional energy security and connectivity.  We also welcome upcoming undersea cables projects in the Indian Ocean which are intended to strengthen regional connectivity. We acknowledge the rapid increase in the number and scale of cyber incidents in the region and announce enhanced Quad Cybersecurity Cooperation , through which we plan to work together to achieve an open and secure cyberspace. We unequivocally condemn terrorism and violent extremism in all its forms and manifestations, including cross-border terrorism, and commit to strengthening the Quad’s ongoing cooperation on counterterrorism. We reaffirm our unwavering support for ASEAN centrality and unity.  Together, we are committed to upholding a free and open Indo-Pacific. * In Australia, India, and Japan, ‘Super Intelligence’ refers to ‘artificial intelligence.’ The post Quad Leaders’ Summit Joint Press Release appeared first on The White House .

title: Finland’s Iceye bids €2 billion for Italian rocket maker Avio
zh_title: 芬兰 Iceye 出价 20 亿欧元收购意大利火箭制造商 Avio
summary: 罗马——芬兰运营商 Iceye 向意大利火箭制造商 Avio 提出了 20 亿欧元现金报价（合 22 亿美元），该报价将整合欧洲的太空能力，并让 Iceye 负责 Avio 向美国导弹业务的扩张。拟议的交易符合减少对外部供应商的依赖并缩小与美国和中国行业领导者之间日益扩大的差距的努力。 “欧洲对主权太空和国防能力的需求正在增长。满足这一需求的工业能力建设需要数年时间，这使得现在投资至关重要，”Iceye 周二表示。菲
content:
罗马——芬兰运营商 Iceye 向意大利火箭制造商 Avio 提出了 20 亿欧元现金报价（合 22 亿美元），该报价将整合欧洲的太空能力，并让 Iceye 负责 Avio 向美国导弹业务的扩张。拟议的交易符合减少对外部供应商的依赖并缩小与美国和中国行业领导者之间日益扩大的差距的努力。 “欧洲对主权太空和国防能力的需求正在增长。满足这一需求的工业能力建设需要数年时间，这使得现在投资至关重要，”Iceye 周二表示。该公司表示，将在五年内向意大利 Avio 投资 10 亿欧元，以扩大 Avio Vega 火箭的客户群。芬兰政府支持这一提议，芬兰国防部长安蒂·哈卡宁表示，“如果完成……将创建一个全球航天工业参与者，通过它，芬兰和整个欧洲国防的自给自足的供应安全将上升到一个新的水平。” Avio 周二表示正在考虑这一收购要约，而拥有 Avio 18% 股份的意大利国家控股国防集团 Leonardo 的首席执行官表示，他对这一收购要约感到“惊喜”，并将予以考虑。 Avio 董事会于周二举行了第一次会议，并表示已开始评估此次出价，Iceye 表示，该出价较该意大利集团周一收盘价溢价 21.3%，较其三个月成交量加权平均价溢价 34.8%。
除了欧洲航天发射活动外，Avio 也是导弹固体火箭发动机的市场领导者。9 月，该公司在弗吉尼亚州赫特的美国新设施破土动工，以实现为美国导弹生产带来急需的额外产能的雄心。 Avio 已与雷神公司合作生产 Mk 104 双推力火箭发动机，并与洛克希德·马丁公司合作在 Hurt 为洛克希德的增程 GMLRS (ER GMLRS) 和精确打击导弹 (PrSM) 项目生产发动机。 Avio 发言人告诉《防务新闻》，如果 Iceye 收购，则需要美国政府的批准以及意大利政府的批准。 9月，Avio宣布9个月的订单额为2.37亿欧元，其中一半与国防相关，其余主要与其Vega C和Vega E发射器有关。 Iceye 表示，其每股 41 欧元的报价将通过全资意大利子公司 Iris 2 发起，目的是使该公司退市。消息传出后，Avio 股价上涨超过 15%，至 39.5 欧元左右。 Iceye 自 2022 年以来一直向乌克兰提供卫星雷达图像，上个月与诺基亚和乌克兰国防部签署了一份意向书，探讨太空合作，包括主权卫星通信。
Iceye首席执行官拉法尔·莫德热夫斯基(Rafal Modrzewski)在赫尔辛基的一次活动上发表讲话时表示，该公司在发起竞标之前已与包括政府在内的相关各方进行了磋商，并且还需要几个月的时间才能完成交易。“这是一次非凡的能力组合……遵循相当明确的行业趋势，带来了全面的垂直整合，”莫德热夫斯基表示，并补充说这对两家公司都有利。材料来自路透社，作者 Giulia Segreti 和 Essi Lehto。

【原文 English Original】
ROME — Finnish operator Iceye has a made €2 billion cash offer ($2.2 billion) for Italian rocket maker Avio which would integrate Europe’s space capabilities as well as putting Iceye in charge of Avio’s expansion into the U.S. missile business. The proposed deal fits with efforts to reduce reliance on external providers and narrow a widening gap with industry leaders in the U.S. and China. “Europe’s need for sovereign space and defense capabilities is growing. Building the industrial capacity to meet that demand takes years, which makes it critical to invest now,” said Iceye on Tuesday. The firm said it would invest €1 billion in Avio in Italy over five years in a bid to expand the customer base of Avio’s Vega rocket. The Finnish government backed the offer, with Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen stating, “If completed … a global space industry player will be created, through which the self-sufficient security of supply of Finland’s and all of Europe’s defense will rise to a new level.” Avio said on Tuesday it was considering the offer, while the CEO of Italian state controlled defense group Leonardo, which owns an 18% percent stake in Avio, said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the bid and would consider it. Avio’s board held a first meeting on Tuesday and said it had started assessing the bid, which Iceye said offered a 21.3% premium to the Italian group’s closing price on Monday or a 34.8% premium to its three-month volume-weighted average price. Apart from its European space launch activity, Avio is also a market leader in solid rocket motors for missiles. In September it broke ground in Hurt, Virginia, on a new U..S facility to fulfill an ambition to bring much needed extra capacity to U.S. missile production. Avio has already partnered with Raytheon on production of the Mk 104 dual-thrust rocket motor and has teamed with Lockheed Martin to produce motors at Hurt for Lockheed’s Extended Range GMLRS (ER GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) programs. An Avio spokesman told Defense News that U.S. government approval would be required in the event of a takeover by Iceye, as well as Italian government approval. In September, Avio announced a nine month order intake of €237 million, of which half was defense related, with the remainder mainly related to its Vega C and Vega E launchers. Iceye said its €41-per-share offer will be launched through wholly owned Italian subsidiary Iris 2 with the aim of delisting the company. Avio shares climbed more than 15% to around €39.5 on the news. Iceye has supplied Ukraine with satellite radar imagery since 2022, and last month signed a letter of intent with Nokia and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry to explore cooperation in space, including sovereign satellite communications. Speaking at an event in Helsinki, Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction. “It’s a phenomenal combination of capabilities … bringing a full vertical integration, following quite clear industry trends,” Modrzewski said, adding that it would be beneficial for both companies. With material from Reuters by Giulia Segreti and Essi Lehto.

title: Trump seeks nuclear cuts at summit with Putin and Xi, but prospects are low
zh_title: 特朗普在与普京和习近平的峰会上寻求削减核武器，但前景渺茫
summary: 维也纳——美国、俄罗斯和中国领导人将于周四在中国科技大都市深圳会面，这场会议被各方誉为“历史性”会议。讨论的主题包括削减全球核库存。但专家警告说，虽然会议本身是一个积极的进展，但任何重大突破仍然不太可能。过去一周，人们对这次聚会的期望不断升高，尤其是在俄罗斯，该活动被赋予了“雅尔塔2.0”的色彩，指的是1945年重新安排的会议。
content:
维也纳——美国、俄罗斯和中国领导人将于周四在中国科技大都市深圳会面，这场会议被各方誉为“历史性”会议。讨论的主题包括削减全球核库存。但专家警告说，虽然会议本身是一个积极的进展，但任何重大突破仍然不太可能。过去一周，人们对这次聚会的期望不断升高，尤其是在俄罗斯，这次活动被赋予了“雅尔塔2.0”的色彩，指的是1945年二战后重新安排世界秩序的会议。与此同时，从美国方面来看，特朗普政府在深圳推动有关削减核武器的讨论，令许多观察家感到惊讶。俄罗斯和美国之间的最后一项战略军备控制条约（《新削减战略武器条约》）于 2 月到期，这使得这两个最大的核国家自 1972 年以来首次对原子武库没有数量限制。与此同时，中国不是《新削减战略武器条约》的缔约国，事实上也从未加入过任何类似的战略武器条约。据估计，北京拥有世界第三大核武库，有数百个，尽管分析人士认为，中国近年来一直在努力大幅增加这一数字。美国和俄罗斯各自拥有约 4,000 件核武器库存。
这种数字上的差异也是中国此前对以三边形式讨论战略武器限制的想法感到愤怒的原因，就像美国总统唐纳德·特朗普在会议前夕推动的那样。尽管北京方面已经确认了此次会议，但并未正式表示战略武器对话将提上议程。中国外交部发言人毛宁表示，“三位元首将就维护世界和平、促进大国关系战略稳定深入交换意见。”这避免了明确指出美国的要求。 “总统已明确表示，除其他议题外，他将讨论世界范围内核武器的削减。特朗普总统认为，这种扩散非常危险，”白宫发言人奥利维亚·威尔士上周五告诉记者。总部位于维也纳的开放核网络（一家处理核军备控制问题的国际非政府组织）的研究协调员尼基塔·杰格蒂亚列夫（Nikita Degtyarev）表示，他对可实现的成果持现实态度。 “我没有很高的期望，但我很高兴这一切正在发生，”他在接受采访时说。 “领导人级别的会议不同于正在进行的五常对话和其他现有形式。”五常对话汇集了五个核不扩散条约承认的核武器国家——美国、俄罗斯、中国、法国和英国。
– 在工作层面上讨论核政策和降低风险。“如果三边会议就核问题取得任何成果，那它可能更像是一份政治声明，而不是可核查和限制性的军控协议，”核问题项目主任、华盛顿智库战略与国际研究中心高级研究员希瑟·威廉姆斯说，“我认为最有可能的重大成果将是重申里根-戈尔巴乔夫的口头禅，即核战争不可能获胜，也决不能打。”杰格佳廖夫说道。达成更具实质性或开创性的协议也不太可能，因为根本没有

【原文 English Original】
VIENNA — The leaders of the U.S., Russia and China are set to meet in the Chinese tech metropolis of Shenzhen on Thursday in an event that has been hailed as “historic” by all sides. Among the topics raised for discussion are reductions in global nuclear stockpiles. But experts caution that while the meeting itself is a positive development, any major breakthrough remains unlikely.  Expectations for the get-together ratcheted up over the course of the past week, particularly in Russia, where the event has been ascribed undertones of a “Yalta 2.0,” referencing the 1945 conference that reordered the world after World War II. From the U.S. side, meanwhile, the Trump administration surprised many observers by pushing for discussions about reducing nuclear weapons while in Shenzhen. The last strategic arms control treaty between Russia and the U.S., in the form of New START, expired in February, leaving the two largest nuclear states without numerical limits on atomic arsenals  for the first time since 1972.  China, meanwhile, was not a party to New START and was, in fact, never part of any strategic arms treaty like it. Beijing is estimated to have the third-largest nuclear arsenal in the world, at several hundred, although analysts believe it has been working to significantly increase this number in recent years. The U.S. and Russia each have stockpiles of around 4,000  nuclear weapons.  This numerical discrepancy is also why China has previously bristled at the idea of discussing strategic arms limitation in a trilateral format like the one U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing in the run-up to the meeting. Although Beijing has confirmed the meeting, it has stopped short of officially saying strategic arms dialogue would be on the agenda. “The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations,” said Mao Ning, spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry.  This avoids naming explicitly what the U.S. has asked for. “The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told reporters last Friday.  Nikita Degtyarev, research coordinator at the Vienna-based Open Nuclear Network, an international NGO dealing with nuclear arms control, said he was realistic about achievable outcomes. “I don’t have very high expectations, but I’m happy that it’s happening,” he said in an interview. “A meeting at the leader level is something else than the ongoing P5 dialogue and other existing formats.” The P5 dialogue brings together the five Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty-recognized nuclear weapons states – the U.S., Russia, China, France and the U.K. – on a working level to discuss nuclear policy and risk reduction.  “If there is any outcome of the trilateral meeting relating to nuclear issues, it will likely be more of a political statement than a verifiable and restrictive arms control agreement,” said Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues and senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank CSIS ,  “I think the most likely significant outcome would be a reiteration of the Reagan-Gorbachev mantra that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” Degtyarev said. A more substantive or groundbreaking agreement was also unlikely because there simply wasn’t enough time for lower-level officials to hammer out the details of any possible agreement that the leaders could sign, he said. Major arms control treaties often take years of meticulous crafting at the working level before heads of state come together to sign them.  Trump first raised the topic of denuclearization in the context of the summit to reporters on Oct. 19, a day after the Wall Street Journal first reported about a proposed trilateral meeting.  A possible wildcard agenda item remains in the form of artificial intelligence in nuclear weapons. AI in nuclear command and control has emerged as a somewhat more promising topic and a potential area for agreement more palatable to all sides than commitments to numerical reductions or verification mechanisms. The South China Morning Post reported Nov. 11, citing sources familiar with preparations, that working-level teams had discussed AI in critical weapons systems and that the agenda was shifting toward potential common ground, particularly AI’s role in nuclear command and control. One source characterized AI governance of nuclear weapons as an “easy deliverable” consistent with past policies. This “could give Trump something to announce without requiring anyone to compromise their nuclear posture,” Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, told the French press agency AFP .  Under the previous U.S. administration, Biden and Xi reaffirmed the importance of human decision-making in nuclear command and control in November 2024, while Russia has so far resisted such language, including in the P5 process.  Much may depend on the willingness of Beijing to engage in strategic arms dialogue, which has indicated it has no major desire to discuss this topic while China remains a numerical underdog in the quantity of its warheads. “China is the host and will probably closely stage-manage the event and the agenda,” Degtyarev said. Xi Jinping’s style of international engagements tends to be highly scripted and predictable, at odds with Trump’s more improvisational approach.  The common denominator for all three leaders is more likely to be good publicity. “Trump is probably genuine about his interest in nuclear arms reduction,” Degtyarev assessed, “but probably also from a self-serving and PR point of view.”  Though the meeting is historic in nature for its assembling of a triumvirate of the world’s most powerful men, “the Yalta 2.0 comparisons are overblown,” said Degtyarev. “The scale of the historical moment is simply different.”

title: New pact positions the Philippines as a defense hub for Australian troops
zh_title: 新协议将菲律宾定位为澳大利亚军队的防御中心
summary: 菲律宾马尼拉——澳大利亚和菲律宾高级官员签署了一项防务协议，以加速军事协调，为轮换部队部署和澳大利亚对菲律宾军事基础设施的投资铺平道路。 11 月 15 日签署的防务合作协议（DCA）旨在消除行政瓶颈并创建更有效的协调系统，以快速跟踪双边防务活动。到目前为止，两国的军事交流基本上是根据1995年的协议备忘录进行的，而部队交流则以互访地位为指导。
content:
菲律宾马尼拉——澳大利亚和菲律宾高级官员签署了一项防务协议，以加速军事协调，为轮换部队部署和澳大利亚对菲律宾军事基础设施的投资铺平道路。 11 月 15 日签署的防务合作协议（DCA）旨在消除行政瓶颈并创建更有效的协调系统，以快速跟踪双边防务活动。到目前为止，两国的军事交流主要根据1995年的协议备忘录进行，而部队交流则以2007年签署并自2012年起生效的《访问部队地位协议》为指导。据澳大利亚国防部称，新协议涵盖情报共享、军事训练、空中和地面无人机的转让、海上活动和军事基础设施。副总理理查德·马勒斯在一份声明中表示：“这项新的防务合作安排将深化我们国防军之间的务实合作，并为共同支持地区安全创造新的机会。”菲律宾国防部长吉尔伯托·特奥多罗表示，新的 DCA 减少了官僚主义障碍，特别是在部队部署方面，并使澳大利亚能够迅速部署部队来援助菲律宾的救灾工作。特奥多罗在签约后对记者表示：“做一件事不再是 100 个步骤，而是现在只需要 10 个……而且这将更有目的性，而不是临时性的。”
此举正值澳大利亚重新调整其防御态势，以应对中国在印太地区不断扩大的军事能力、不断扩大的导弹射程以及越来越多地使用灰色地带战术和经济胁迫。菲律宾总统小费迪南德·马科斯（中）和第一夫人路易丝·阿拉内塔-马科斯（右）在 11 月 16 日于马尼拉举行的第 49 届东南亚国家联盟 (ASEAN) 峰会期间的晚宴前欢迎澳大利亚总理安东尼·阿尔巴内斯 (Anthony Albanese)。 2026 年。（Nhac Nguyen / POOL / 法新社，盖蒂图片社）“从澳大利亚的角度来看，菲律宾是我们的第一道防线，”澳大利亚战略政策研究所高级研究员尤安·格雷厄姆告诉《防务新闻》。澳大利亚遭受了解放军部队的骚扰，包括危险的海上演习、在其北部专属经济区进行激光瞄准，以及在澳大利亚皇家海军舰艇附近使用声纳和照明弹。与澳大利亚一样，菲律宾也面临着中国的压力。中国船只使用高能水炮、军用级激光，撞击和攻击菲律宾武装部队船只和人员。当被问及 DCA 是否旨在增强台湾海峡的威慑力时，特奥多罗强调该协议将增强“西菲律宾海”和“菲律宾领土”的威慑力。战略转变 澳大利亚标志着和平时期向 2023 年否认战略的历史性转变，最近将其写入 2026 年国防战略。
这个想法是将澳大利亚国防军重塑为一支一体化、集中的军队，能够威慑和阻止其进入其北部通道，其中包括部署前沿防御部队。今年早些时候，澳大利亚在总部位于布里斯班的第18保障旅下成立了新的濒海机动大队，以向更北的地区作战，使菲律宾成为该战略的重要组成部分。但分析师格雷厄姆警告称，澳大利亚只能部署小型部队。并保留这些莫

【原文 English Original】
MANILA, Philippines — Top officials from Australia and the Philippines have inked a defense pact to accelerate military coordination, paving the way for rotational troop deployment and Australian investments in Philippine military infrastructure. The Nov. 15 Defense Cooperation Agreement, or DCA, is designed to cut administrative bottlenecks and create a more efficient coordination system to fast-track bilateral defense activities. So far the two countries’ military exchanges have largely fallen under a 1995 memorandum of agreement, while troop exchanges were guided by the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement, signed in 2007 and effective since 2012. According to Australia’s Department of Defence, the new pact covers intelligence-sharing, military training, the transfer of aerial and surface drones, maritime activities, and military infrastructure. “This new Defence Cooperation Arrangement will deepen practical cooperation between our defense forces and create new opportunities to work together in support of regional security,” Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said in a statement. Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said the new DCA reduces bureaucratic barriers, particularly in troop deployment, and would allow Australia to rapidly deploy troops to aid in Philippine disaster response. “Rather than 100 steps to do a single thing, it will just now take 10 … and it will be more purposeful and not ad hoc,” Teodoro told reporters following the signing. The move comes as Australia recalibrates its defense posture in response to China’s expanding military capabilities, growing missile reach, and increasing use of gray-zone tactics and economic coercion in the Indo-Pacific. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (C) and First Lady Louise Araneta-Marcos (R) welcome Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ahead of the Gala Dinner during the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 16, 2026. (Nhac Nguyen / POOL / AFP via Getty Images) “From Australia’s point of view, the Philippines is our first line of defense,” Australian Strategic Policy Institute senior fellow Euan Graham told Defense News. Australia has experienced harassment by PLA forces, including dangerous maritime maneuvers, laser targeting in its northern exclusive economic zone, and the use of sonar and flares in close proximity to Royal Australian Navy vessels. Like Australia, the Philippines faces Chinese pressure head-on. Chinese ships have used high-powered water cannons, pointed military-grade lasers, rammed, and attacked Armed Forces of the Philippines vessels and personnel. When asked if the DCA was meant to boost deterrence in the Taiwan Strait, Teodoro emphasized the agreement will bolster “deterrence in the West Philippine Sea” and in “Philippine territory.” Strategy shift Australia marked a historic peacetime shift toward a strategy of denial in 2023, most recently codified in the 2026 national defense strategy. The idea is to reshape the Australian Defense Force into an integrated, focused military capable of deterring and denying access to its northern approaches, which includes deploying a forward-defense force. Earlier this year, Australia created the new Littoral Maneuver Group under the 18th Sustainment Brigade headquartered in Brisbane, to operate farther north, making the Philippines an important part of that strategy. But Australia can only deploy small units, analyst Graham cautioned. And keeping these mobile forces supplied and operational in archipelagic countries like the Philippines is challenging, as troops and equipment are moved across widely dispersed islands during operations. Building logistics networks To that end, the new cooperation agreement is expected to facilitate discussions on potential Australian investments in Philippine military infrastructure. A list of five Luzon bases slated to receive funding for eight infrastructure projects was expected to be finalized around August this year. However, only one base has been discussed in detail so far, officials told Defense News. Teodoro previously clarified that base agreements with Australia will follow a different model than the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) between the Philippines and the United States, which includes provisions for prepositioning military equipment and assets. The Australian “basing” arrangements, officials said, would include areas that are not traditional bases. Rather than a large basing presence, what the Australian military needs is access to locations that could sustain its forces during operations and contingencies. Discussions so far have included sustainment and logistics to support joint operations while troops spread across the archipelago’s most complex, most challenging, and remote terrains. Graham said Australia’s role in the Philippines is distinct but complementary to that of the United States. While physical locations could overlap, the infrastructure projects would be different.  Canberra and Manila in 2021 signed the Mutual Support Logistics Arrangement, which covers fuel and other supplies for aircraft and vessels, transportation, logistics, and coordination. “The importance of logistics can’t be underestimated. It’s not just about getting your fighting force fighting. You’ve got to supply them with food, fuel, and ammunition during all of that,” Graham said. More complex training With the new DCA with Australia in place, joint exercises , especially Exercise ALON, will see a larger iteration next year, Teodoro said. Exercise ALON, first held in 2023, is the biennial flagship joint training exercise between countries, focused on amphibious operations. The 2025 edition saw Australia’s largest overseas military exercise for the year and showcased the ADF projecting combat forces into the contested West Philippine Sea, Graham said. Apart from maritime training, Teodoro said there will be more aerial, land, cyber, and multidomain training exercises between Filipino and Australian troops. Military officials told Defense News that Army training has been a priority area for the Australian military’s training playbook in the Philippines. The focus follows sweeping changes in both countries’ land forces to prepare them for modern conflicts. While the Philippine Army expands from its signature jungle and urban warfare expertise toward coastal defense, the Australian ground service has pivoted toward littoral warfare. Since 2023, exchanges have focused on techniques, tactics, and procedures for amphibious operations, Army spokesperson Col. Louie Dema-ala told Defense News. But future iterations will include advanced training, Dema-ala said. “We are transitioning into a multi-domain capable Army.” The exchange is not one-sided. Australia also stands to benefit from the Philippine Army’s experience operating in dense jungle terrain. “This is not just a one-way process. We can learn from the jungle warfare fighting skills, and I think that’s important to stress. No one can tell us about the Philippines better than the Filipinos,” Graham said.
